title: Regulating electrochemical CO2RR selectivity at industrial current densities by structuring copper@poly(ionic liquid) interface
abstract: Ionic liquid-based electrocatalytic CO2 reduction faces the challenge of achieving high selectivity toward valueadded C2+ products at high reaction rate (≥ 100 mA cm 2). Herein, novel copper@poly(ionic liquid) (Cu@PIL) hybrids demonstrate multi-electron reduction (> 2e–) with current densities ≥ 300 mA cm 2. Remarkably, Cu@PIL with F– anion exhibits high C2+ faradaic efficiency of 58 % with a high partial current density of 174 mA cm 2. Further, a highest C2+ partial current density of 233 mA cm 2 was also achieved. Experimental combined theoretical investigations reveal that the “individual” ionic pairs in the outer PIL layer enrich local CO2 concentration, thereby promoting the CO2 supply. Besides, an interfacial electric field is induced by the unbonded imidazolium moieties at Cu-PIL interface, which stabilize intermediates. Anions, differing in the electrondonating number to the imidazolium moieties, influence both the enrichment of CO2 and the stabilization of intermediates, thus regulating current density and product selectivity.

Ionic liquid-based electrocatalytic CO2 reduction faces the challenge of achieving high selectivity toward valueadded C2+ products at high reaction rate (≥ 100 mA cm− 2). Herein, novel copper@poly(ionic liquid) (Cu@PIL) hybrids demonstrate multi-electron reduction (> 2e–) with current densities ≥ 300 mA cm− 2. Remarkably, Cu@PIL with F– anion exhibits high C2+ faradaic efficiency of 58 % with a high partial current density of 174 mA cm− 2. Further, a highest C2+ partial current density of 233 mA cm− 2 was also achieved. Experimental combined theoretical investigations reveal that the “individual” ionic pairs in the outer PIL layer enrich local CO2 concentration, thereby promoting the CO2 supply. Besides, an interfacial electric field is induced by the unbonded imidazolium moieties at Cu-PIL interface, which stabilize intermediates. sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Continuous emissions of carbon dioxide (CO2) have led to remarkable climate changes [1,2]. Converting CO2 into high value-added chemicals and fuels was therefore regarded as one of the most promising technology to realize a sustainable carbon-neutral cycle [3,4]. To date, a variety of technologies on using CO2 as the C1 surrogate in the chemical synthesis have been documented [5–8]. Therein, the environmentally friendly electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) attracts the most attention [9]. During the past decade, many efforts and thus phenomenal progress in electrocatalyst [10–13], electro-catalyzer [14], and electrolyte [15] have been made to achieve high-performance CO2RR. Remarkably, ionic liquids (ILs) are considered as the ideal medium for high-efficiency CO2RR owing to the intrinsic properties, such as high CO2 solubility [16–19], high CO2-activate ability [20–22], high stability [23], and wide electrochemical windows [15]. For instance, Vedharathinam et al. [24] employed a porous Ag foam as the cathode and got a high carbon monoxide (CO) faradaic efficiency (FE) of 75 % with a current density of
36.6 mA cm− 2 in an electrolyte comprising 92 vol% 1-ethyl-3-methylimidazolium tetrafluoroborate ([Emim]BF4) and 8 vol% water. By conducting 1-benzyl-3-methylimidazolium tetrafluoroborate ([Bzmim]BF4)-H2O-acetonitrile ternary mixture as the electrolyte, formate (HCOO–) was generated with a high FE of 92.7 % and a current density of 30.5 mA cm− 2 on Pb-based electrocatalyst [25]. Despite many encouraging achievements that have been obtained in the IL-mediated CO2RR, the current data is not enough to support its leap from the lab to industry [26–29]. The major issue of this field is the present low selectivity toward high value-added C2+ products [15,30]. Only those of C1, such as methanol, in IL medium have been obtained even by launching Cu-based materials, which is regarded as the most promising catalyst for C–C coupling [31]. It’s attributed to the low stabilization of key intermediates, such as the adsorbed CO (*CO), at the IL-metal interface [32]. Challenges also include making the current density satisfy the requirement of industrial applications (e.g. over a hundred mA cm− 2) [33]. The documented low value (< 40 mA cm− 2) [15] is imposed by the high viscosity of ILs, which results in not only high cell resistance but also poor mass transfer.

On the other hand, recent documents demonstrated the polymermetal hybrids could alter the performance of CO2RR by both affecting the properties of metal surfaces and changing the local chemical environment near the catalytic site [34–37]. We, thus, envisioned the preparation of core-shell metal@poly(ionic liquid) (M@PIL) hybrids and their application in the CO2RR. The PILs of specific spatial structures have been well explored in the thermo-catalysis of CO2 transformation due to the ionic nature, high density of catalytic sites, and tunable construction [38–40]. As compared to the bulk ILs, PILs keep the ionic moieties and accessible basic groups (amines, imines, triazines, carbazoles, imidazoles, and azo linkages), while they also possess the high specific surface area, flourishing porosity structure, and relative rigid skeleton [41]. All these properties exert important effects on the adsorption of CO2, thereby facilitating its transformation. In this regard, the outer layer of PIL in M@PIL is designed as the channel for CO2 transport based on the strong IL− CO2 interaction [15], while the M-PIL interface (or inner layer of PIL) could function as the catalytic sites with the interfacial electric field induced by PIL [32]. Moreover, anions in the PIL with different steric hindrances are assumed to influence both the CO2 transport and the interfacial electric field via anion-cation interaction, thus adjusting the reactants supply and the stabilization of intermediates. Besides, a flow cell equipped with a gas diffusion electrode (GDE) also employed to speed up the mass transfer and lower the resistance. By implementing such a strategy, industrial current densities with tunable selectivity of CO2RR could be achieved.
To test our hypothesis, a novel IL-X (X = F–, Cl–, Br–, I–, BF4–, PF6–) monomer (Scheme 1) comprising a tridentate site, consisting of one pyridinic and two imidazolium groups, and two vinyl sits for polymerization was synthesized. The subsequent in-situ radical polymerization of IL-X in the presence of copper nanoparticles (Cu NPs) provides the corresponding core-shell Cu@PIL-X hybrids. The desired organicinorganic interfacial structure was obtained through strong coordination of the tridentate site in PIL to the surficial Cu atoms. Besides, the density of the PIL shell therein could be readily adjusted by the molar ratio of IL-X to the Cu NPs. To our delight, superior current densities (≥300 mA cm− 2) that higher than those in most flow cells [42] are obtained with such a Cu@PIL catalytic system. Moreover, all Cu@PIL hybrids under screening exhibit the capability to reduce CO2 in-depth (> 2e–), while the anion has a significant impact on the product distribution of CO2RR. Representatively, Cu@PIL-F exhibits a high C2+ FE of 58 % with a high partial current density of 174 mA cm-2 (in 3 M KOH), while the main products on Cu@PIL-Cl and Cu@PIL-Br were ethylene (C2H4, FE = 29 %) and methane (CH4, FE = 35 %), respectively. The highest current density of ~590 mA cm− 2 with a low H2 FE (~22 %) was achieved at –1.25 V (vs. reversible hydrogen electrode, RHE; the same below) on Cu@PIL-F. The combination of experimental exploration and theoretic calculation disclosed that the high current densities are attributed to the CO2 enrichment promoted by the “individual” ionic pairs in the outer PIL layer. Besides, the interfacial electric field was imposed by the imidazolium cation which is “forced” to approach the Cu
surface by a rigid skeleton of PIL and thus stabilizes the polarized intermediates during the electrolysis. Importantly, the Cu@PIL-X differs in both the CO2 enrichment and intermediate stabilization since the electron-donating number from the respective anion to the imidazolium counterpart is different, thereby regulating the current density and product selectivity accordingly. Finally, the reaction routes with *CO as the key intermediate is proposed, which further signifies the anion effects on the product distribution.

sections.heading: 2.1. General procedures for preparation of Cu@PIL
sections.text:
Cu@PIL hybrids were prepared by the addition of Cu NPs to a solution of vinyl-decorated IL monomer, cross-linking agent, and initiator, followed by in-situ polymerization. The resulted hybrids are denoted as Cu@PIL-X-N, wherein X represents the anion structure in IL-X (X = F–, Cl–, Br–, I–, BF4–, PF6–) and N denotes the molar ratio of IL monomer to Cu NPs for the synthesis. Taking Cu@PIL-F-1.2 as an example, IL-F (0.396 g, 1.2 mmol, 1 equiv.), divinylbenzene (DVB, 0.312 g, 2.4 mmol, 2 equiv.), and azodiisobutyronitrile (AIBN, 0.020 g, 5 wt%) were dissolved in methanol (30 mL) under Ar atmosphere. After stirring at room temperature for 1 h, the mixture was heated to reflux at 85 ◦C for 1.5 h, and a suspension of Cu NPs (0.128 g, 2 mmol, 1.67 equiv.) in methanol (10 mL) was added dropwise. After refluxing for a further 24 h, the mixture was filtrated. The residue was washed with methanol (10 mL × 5), followed by drying under vacuum to afford Cu@PIL-F-1.2 as a brown solid.
The procedure for the synthesis of Cu@PIL-X-1.2 with other anions (X = Cl–, Br–, I–, BF4–, PF6–) is similar, in which IL monomer with the corresponding anion is used and the solution is dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) for BF4– and PF6–. For Cu@PIL-F-N (N = 0.3, 0.6, and 2.4), the different mole of IL-F was added. When preparing pure PIL-F, no Cu NPs were added while the rest of the operations are the same as those of Cu@PIL-F-1.2.

sections.heading: 2.2. Preparation of GDE loaded with Cu@PIL
sections.text:
Cu@PIL with different anions were deposited on the microporous layer (MPL) of a commercial carbon paper (29BCE, Sigracet) by a modified airbrushing method [43]. Typically, Cu@PIL NPs (10 mg) were added to a dispersion liquid consisting of isopropanol (4000 μL) and Nafion perfluorosulfonic acid (PFSA) polymer dispersions (63 μL, 5 wt %). The mixture was sonicated for 1 h to make a uniform catalyst ink. The as-prepared ink was sprayed onto carbon paper (8.3 × 1 cm− 2) on a hot plate of 90 ◦C with an airbrush gun (Infinity-CR PLUS 0.4, HARDER & STEENBECK) at the distance of 10 cm. The catalyst loading is around 1.2 mg cm− 2.

sections.heading: 2.3. Electrochemical studies
sections.text:
All the electrochemical studies, including linear sweep voltammetry (LSV), electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), and electrolysis, were conducted in a homemade three-chamber flow cell (Fig. S10). The dimensions of the gas chamber are 2.0 × 0.5 × 0.15 cm3, while the catholyte and anolyte chambers are larger (2.0 × 0.5 × 0.3 cm3). GDE loaded with Cu@PIL (1.0 cm2) was the working electrode which was set up between the gas and catholyte chambers. A piece of Ni foam (2.5 × 1.5 × 0.16 cm3) was used as the counter electrode. An anion exchange membrane (FAA-3-PK-130, Fumasep) was placed between the catholyte and anolyte chambers. Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) gaskets were used to seal and fix the electrodes. Aqueous KOH solution (1 M) was used as the electrolyte with the catholyte and anolyte flow rates of 1 mL min− 1 and 20 mL min− 1, respectively. The inlet CO2 flow rate was set as 11.5 mL min− 1, while the flow rate at the outlet was measured by a soap film flowmeter. An external mercuric oxide (Hg/HgO/OH-, 1 M KOH) electrode reference electrode was used to measure the cathodic potential. All the measured cathodic potentials were converted to RHE (ERHE) with iR (85 %) compensations using the following equation:
ERHE = Eref + 0.098(V) + 0.059(V) × pH - iR × 85%
where Eref is the measured cathodic potential, i is the average current density during the test, and R is the solution resistance measured by the EIS test (Fig. S41, S42, and Table S11). For LSV test and electrolysis at lower current density (≤ 400 mA cm− 2), an Autolab PGSTAT204 N workstation (Metrohm, Switzerland) was employed, while a CS150H workstation (CorrTest, China) was used at ≥ 400 mA cm− 2.

sections.heading: 2.4. Product quantification
sections.text:
Gaseous products during electrolysis were quantified using an online 8890 gas chromatography (GC) system (Agilent, USA) at intervals of 15 min. H2 and CO were quantified using a thermal conductivity detector (TCD) equipped with HyaesepQ and Molsieve 5 Å columns. CH4, C2H6, and C2H4 were quantified using a flame ionization detector (FID) equipped with an HP-PLOT Al2O3 column. The chromatograms of standard samples and corresponding calibration curves are shown in Fig. S11 and Fig. S12. The Faradaic efficiency (FEg) for gaseous products was calculated using the following equation:
FEg = z × F × xg × f
i × 100%
where z is the electron transfer number (z of different products see supplementary material), F is the Faraday constant (96485 C mol− 1), xg is the mole fraction of the product, f is the flow rate at the outlet (L s− 1), and i is the current (A).
Liquid products were quantified using an AVIII 600 nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectrometer (Bruker, Germany). After electrolysis (4200 s), 400 μL of catholyte was mix with 200 μL D2O containing 25 ppm (m/m) DMSO and 250 ppm (m/m) phenol as internal standards, and the peak area ratio of product and standard were used for quantification. The 1H NMR spectra of standard samples and corresponding calibration curves are shown in Fig. S13 and Fig. S14. The Faradaic efficiency (FEl) for liquid products was calculated using the following equation:
FEl = z × F × cl × V
Q × 100%
where cl is the measured concentration of liquid product (mol mL− 1), V is the volume of catholyte (50 mL), Q is the practical electricity consumed during electrolysis (C).

sections.heading: 2.5. In situ Raman studies during CO2RR
sections.text: A custom-made electrochemical Raman flow cell (Fig. S28) was used for the in-situ Raman test. A Graphite rod and a mercuric oxide (Hg/ HgO/OH− , KOH (1 M)) electrode was used as the counter and reference electrodes, respectively. GDE loaded with Cu@PIL-F-1.2 was the working electrode. An anion exchange membrane (FAA-3-PK-130, Fumasep) was placed between the catholyte and anolyte chambers. Aqueous KOH solution (1 M) was used as the electrolyte with a high flow rate of 50 mL min− 1 to remove the H2 bubbles on the cathode. CO2 with an inlet flow rate of 35 mL min-1 was introduced into the gas chamber at the backside of GDE. All electrochemical tests were performed with a CS150H workstation (CorrTest, China). The Raman test was conducted on an inVia Qontor confocal Raman microscope (Renishaw, UK) equipped with a 785 nm laser and a 50× objective.

sections.heading: 3.1. Characterization of Cu@PIL
sections.text:
The morphology of Cu@PIL was characterized by the high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and the scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (Fig. 1a~1f, S1~S2). Taking Cu@PIL-F-1.2 as an example, the TEM image suggests it has a typical core-shell structure (Fig. 1a~1e). At the surface of Cu NPs, a thin layer of amorphous PIL can be defined. The lattice distance of 0.21 nm (Fig. 1a and 1b), assigned to the typical (111) inter-planar distance of Cu metal, suggests the maintenance of the Cu NPs structure upon modification. The TEM images also reveal the uniform distribution of Cu@PIL-F-1.2 particles (Fig. S1) with an average PIL thickness of ~10 nm. Both TEM (Fig. 1a and S1) and SEM (Fig. 1f) images demonstrate the particle size of Cu@PIL-F-1.2 is less than 50 nm. In comparison, Cu@PIL-X-1.2 (X = Cl–, Br–, and I–) hybrids have similar morphologies as that of Cu@PIL-F-1.2, while Cu@PIL-BF41.2 and Cu@PIL-PF6-1.2 aggregate slightly (Fig. S2). The powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) profile of Cu@PIL-X-1.2 hybrids (Fig. S3) and those loaded on the MPL of GDE (Fig. 1g) have the typical pattern of Cu metal, confirming the PIL layer is thin and amorphous. Evidently, the crosssectional SEM images (Fig. 1h, 1i, S4, and S5) demonstrate a highly loose and porous structure of Cu@PIL-X-1.2 loaded on the MPL of GDE, thus persisting abundant catalytic sites and facilitating the mass transfer.
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) spectra were carried out to explore the interfacial properties of Cu@PIL-X-1.2 imposed by the difference in incidence depth of X-ray in polymer and metal (Fig. S6). Specifically, Cu LMM Auger spectra (Fig. 2a) were employed to identify Cu species due to the indiscernible features in Cu 2p XPS spectra (Fig. S7). As is shown, the LMM Auger spectrum of Cu NPs (dark grey line) comprises five atomic multiple features, including the 3F peak at the kinetic energy (KE) of ~921 eV [44], the 1S peak with the corresponding shoulder peak at the KE of 912.0 eV–913.0 eV [45], and three intense peaks at 918.7 eV, 916.3 eV, and 918.0 eV assigned to Cu(0) (Cu metal) [46], Cu(I) (Cu2O) [47], and Cu(II) (CuO) [48], respectively. By contrast, all Cu@PIL-X-1.2 hybrids feature a broad peak at ~914 eV, which is assigned to the chelated Cu species with organic ligands [49]. Evidently, the interface of Cu@PIL-X-1.2 is mainly composed of chelated Cu and Cu2O rather than CuO and the neat Cu. Correspondingly, the intensities of typical CuO at the binding energy (BE) of 529.5 eV in the high-resolution O 1s XPS spectra are very weak (Fig. S8) [48]. However, it’s difficult to figure out the charge of each chelated Cu and their ratio at the interface because the recognition of copper-organic complexes by KE locates at a broad range from 912 eV to 915 eV [50,51].
The high-resolution XPS spectra in the N 1s region are displayed in Fig. 2b. The appearance of the peak at the BE of 399.5 eV (assigned to the Cu-chelated pyridinic N) with the same intensity as that at 399.1 eV (assigned to the unbonded pyridinic N) suggests around half of the pyridinic N atoms in the PIL shell has bonded to Cu atoms via

Besides, the other two peaks at over 400.7 eV and 400.0 eV are assigned to the respective N atoms in the imidazolium ring (Fig. 2d, highlighted in dark blue) [54,55] and its carbene derivatives (Fig. 2d, highlighted in light blue) [56,57]. As is shown, the imidazolium fragments in the PIL were only partially converted into the carbene counterparts during the hybridization, followed by coordination to Cu at the interface. We also found the BEs of imidazolium nitrogen shifted gradually from 400.7 eV to 402.0 eV in an order of F– < Cl– < Br– < I– < BF4– < PF6–, corresponding to the reduction of anion-cation interaction strength. The presence of a peak at around 286 eV in the high-resolution C 1s XPS spectra (Fig. 2c) confirms the formation of carbene moieties [56–59]. However, the intensity is so weak that it’s readily overlapped by the neighbour’s strong peak at 284.8 eV that assigned to either C–C or C–H bond in the PIL skeleton [58,59]. Further, XPS analysis (Fig. S9) also confirms each anion is retained during the hybridization.

sections.heading: 3.2. Cu@PIL with different anions for CO2RR
sections.text:
To accelerate mass transfer and diminish cell resistance, a flow cell (Fig. S10) equipped with GDE and anion exchange membrane (AEM) was employed. The electrochemical CO2RR experiments were thereafter performed through steady-state potentiostatic electrolysis in a KOH (1 M) electrolyte solution. The influence of anions (X) in Cu@PIL-X-1.2 on the CO2RR performance and reaction rates were examined at the cathodic potentials range from –0.55 to –0.95 V (Fig. S15). Note that both potentials were set up relative to the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE). At the lower overpotential (–0.55 V, Fig. 3a), a high current density of ~50 mA cm− 2 was obtained for Cu@PIL-F-1.2 with CO (FE of 67.9 %) and HCOO– (FE of 12.6 %) as the major products, demonstrating the interaction between *CO and the catalytic site is weak. By contrast, for Cu@PIL-PF6-1.2, a total C2+ FE of 23.6 % was achieved together with C1 FE of only 22.9 % at a much lower current density of 18.1 mA cm− 2. Besides, the FE of H2 is quite low (only 7.9 %) in the case of Cu@PIL-F-
1.2 during the electrolysis, while more than half of the electrons were consumed to generate H2 for Cu@PIL-PF6-1.2. When the cathodic potential negatively shifted to –0.95 V (Fig. 3b), a similar trend in current density can be observed. It decreases in the order of F– (396.4 mA cm− 2) > Cl– (381.0 mA cm− 2) > Br– (299.8 mA cm− 2) > I– (198.3 mA cm− 2), and then slightly increased for BF4– (230.0 mA cm− 2) and PF6– (249.8 mA cm− 2). The FE of CO on Cu@PIL-F-1.2 is still as high as 35.6 % at a high reaction rate (396.4 mA cm− 2), confirming the readily desorption of *CO at the surface. In comparison, a C2H4 FE of 29.0 % is obtained for Cu@PIL-Cl-1.2 with a high current density (381.0 mA cm− 2). It suggests the surface of Cu@PIL-Cl-1.2 has fairly strong adsorption ability toward *CO, which is indispensable for the C–C coupling for the generation of C2+ products [60]. Finally, Cu@PIL-X-1.2 with the other anions, such as Br–, I–, BF4–, and PF6–, mainly have CH4 selectivity at high overpotential, indicating the adsorption of *CO on these catalysts is even stronger [60].
The above results also indicate the selectivity toward HER for Cu@PIL-X-1.2 varied regularity with different anions as the FE of H2 increases in the order of F– (12.2 %) < Cl– (14.9 %) < Br– (24.4 %) < I– (39.9 %) < BF4– (47.6 %) < PF6– (72.0 %). However, the catalytic activity for HER decreases in the sequence of F– > Cl– > Br– > I– as demonstrated by the LSV test (Fig. 3b, short-dashed curves). Specifically, Cu@PIL-F1.2 has the highest H2 catalytic activity, but with the lowest H2 FE of 12.2 % even at a high current density (396.4 mA cm− 2). Besides, the potential difference at the same current density of 50 mA cm− 2 also decreases in the sequence of F– (171 mV) < Cl– (115 mV) < Br– (84 mV) < I– (40 mV) by comparing HER curves and CO2RR curves (Fig. 3b, short-dashed curves vs. solid curves; and Table S1). We thus attributed the low H2 FE of Cu@PIL-F-1.2 to the superior CO2RR catalytic activity. The comparison between F–, BF4–, and PF6– was also conducted (Fig. 3c). Cu@PIL-BF4-1.2 has a similar HER curve as that of Cu@PIL-F-1.2 but much lower activity towards CO2RR, resulting in totally different catalytic performance. For Cu@PIL-PF6-1.2, the HER and CO2RR curves are very close to each other with a potential difference of 19 mV (Table S1), and both far from those of Cu@PIL-F-1.2, leading to the high FE of H2

influence the mass transfer of the H source (i.e. H2O in this work), thereby affording the respective catalytic performance. To ascertain the high current density of such a system, the wettability of Cu@PIL hybrids was examined (Fig. S16 and Table S2). It shows that Cu@PIL-X-1.2 with anions of F–, Cl–, Br–, and I– are hydrophobic with the contact angle (CA) increasing from 128.9 ± 0.7◦ to 144.0 ± 0.4◦. These results suggest the surface of Cu@PIL-F-1.2 may persist a higher concentration of H source than that of Cu@PIL-I, corresponding to the positive performance of the former in the current density and HER activity. Besides, the mass transfer of CO2 within the electrode is more important for the reaction rate of CO2RR. The CO2-temperature programmed desorption (TPD) analysis of Cu@PIL hybrids was next conducted (Fig. 3d). The presence of intense chemisorption peaks at over 300 ◦C and a broad strong physisorption bond at around 158 ◦C for Cu@PIL-F-1.2 demonstrate the local CO2 concentration around the catalytic sites at the interface is enriched, thus facilitating its transformation. Moreover, both the chemisorption and physisorption are weak for Cu@PIL-X-1.2 other than Cu@PIL-F-1.2, wherein the values for Cu@PIL-BF4-1.2 and Cu@PIL-PF61.2 are extremely poor. Accordingly, Cu@PIL-BF4-1.2 delivers a much lower current density, albeit it has a similar CA (129.2 ± 0.8◦) as Cu@PIL-F-1.2 (Fig. S16 and Table S2).
The difference of the electrochemical surface area (ECSA) for Cu@PIL-X-1.2 is moderate with the anions (Fig. S17, Fig. S18, and Table S3). It suggests ECSA is not the decisive parameter for the current density, although the best Cu@PIL-F-1.2 still has the highest value. To get insight into the kinetics of the generation of CO (or *CO), the Tafel analysis was performed (Fig. 3e). The Tafel slope of Cu@PIL-X-1.2 increases in an order of F– (138 mV dec− 1) < Cl– (190 mV dec− 1) < Br– (212 mV dec− 1) < I– (242 mV dec− 1), signifying the rate-limiting step (RLS) changes with anions in the PIL fragment. Representatively, Cu@PIL-F-1.2 has the Tafel slope of 138 mV dec− 1, which is close to 118 mV dec− 1, suggesting the electron transfer is involved in the RLS [61]. The higher slopes for the other Cu@PIL hybrids demonstrate the reaction therein is mass-transfer limited which is imposed by the slow rate in transferring reactants to the catalytic sites at the surface [62,63].

sections.heading: 3.3. Cu@PIL with different PIL content for CO2RR
sections.text:
To understand the role of the PIL shell at the Cu@PIL hybrids during CO2RR, control experiments were carried out. With cathodic potential at –0.55 V, the performance of blank carbon paper (CP) and PIL-F were initially examined, which all exhibit very poor selectivity to CO2RR (H2 FE > 75 %) (Fig. S19a). However, Cu NPs has a similar product distribution (mainly CO) as compared to Cu@PIL-F-1.2, but with a much lower current density and higher HER selectivity. Upon shifting the cathodic potential to –0.95 V, the difference in current density between Cu@PIL-F-1.2 and Cu NPs is enlarged to over 200 mA cm− 2 (Fig. S19b and S19c), with more C1 product being provided with Cu@PIL-F-1.2. Collectively, these results suggest: i) neither the Cu surface nor the PIL-F layer can account for the catalytic sites of Cu@PIL-F-1.2; ii) the presence of PIL-F shell enriches the reactant around the catalytic sites, thus greatly accelerating the reaction rate; iii) the PIL-F layer could influence the stabilization of intermediates, thus delivering different selectivity. The Cu@PIL-F-1.2 after electrolysis at 300 mA cm− 2 for 1.5 h was characterized by both XRD and XPS (Fig. S20). Compared to the pristine Cu@PIL-F-1.2, the Cu(II) species disappear together with the increase in the intensity of Cu(I) species, suggesting the Cu surface may be dominated with Cu(I)- or Cu(0)-species during the electrolysis. However, Gao’s group recently demonstrated that nano-sized Cu(0)species can be immediately re-oxidized to Cu2O after the applied cathodic potential is removed [64], which means the ex-situ XPS test cannot provide accurate information of Cu surface during CO2RR. To get insight into the oxidation state of Cu during electrolysis, the in-situ Raman was performed and the results will be discussed in Section 3.4.
The performance of Cu@PIL-F-N with different ratios of feedstock (IL-F and Cu NPs) were next examined at the cathodic potentials range from –0.55 to –0.95 V (Fig. S21). At –0.55 V (Fig. 4a), the catalytic performance of Cu@PIL-F-N (N = 0.3, 0.6, 1.2, and 2.4) is similar, mainly delivering C1 product. Notably, the FEs of CH4 and C2H4 are slightly higher on Cu@PIL-F-2.4. When the cathodic potential negatively shifted to –0.95 V (Fig. 4b), the differences in the catalytic performance with the above hybrids are amplified. Specifically, the product distribution on Cu@PIL-F-N (N = 0.3, 0.6, and 1.2) is still comparable, while Cu@PIL-F-2.4 mainly provides CH4. Meanwhile, the current density increased slightly with the molar ratio sequence of 0.3 < 0.6 < 1.2, and then decreased abruptly on Cu@PIL-F-2.4.
The LSV curves of Cu@PIL-F-N with the molar ratio less than 1.2 in the absence of CO2 are almost overlapped (Fig.4b, short-dashed curve), signifying they persist identical HER behavior. In comparison, a high hydrophobicity of surface and low ECSA were obtained for Cu@PIL-F2.4 (Fig. S22, S23, S24, Table S2 and Table S4), which thus significantly inhibit the HER process. In this regard, Cu@PIL-Br-1.2, Cu@PIL-I1.2, and Cu@PIL-PF6-1.2 perform the same. Meanwhile, the LSV curves of Cu@PIL-F-N shift positively with increasing the value of N from 0.3 to 1.2 under CO2 (Fig. 4b, solid curve). As a result, Cu@PIL-F-1.2 has higher CO2RR activity, corresponding to the better total FE of CO2RR and larger current density. By contrast, the CO2RR-related LSV curve of Cu@PIL-F-2.4 significantly negatively shifted. However, the total selectivity toward CO2RR is still high on Cu@PIL-F-2.4, which may be attributed to the high enrichment of CO2 by a thick shell of PIL-F (Fig. 3d).
The Tafel plots of Cu@PIL-F-N were next conducted as displayed in Fig. 4c. The mass transfer of CO2 is promoted with the larger molar ratio (N ≤ 1.2), which is attributed to a thicker coterminous PIL-F layer as CO2 transport channels. However, too much PIL-F may decimate the mass transfer of both the reactant (CO2) and primary product (*CO), resulting in a low current density but high selectivity toward CH4 [35]. As a result, Cu@PIL-F-2.4 exhibits a high CH4 FE of 42 % and a low H2 FE of 16 % with a current density of 265 mA cm− 2 (partial current density of CH4 is 111.3 mA cm− 2). It’s superior to not only those of Cu@PIL-X-1.2 (X = Br, I, and BF4) hybrids in this study but also most of the reported values (Table S8). These results suggest the enhancement of CO2 for mass transfer is vital for improving the overall CO2RR performance.

sections.heading: 3.4. Mechanism and reaction pathway of Cu@PIL catalyzed CO2RR
sections.text:
To date, two hypotheses were used to signify the effect of ILs on the CO2RR process, namely the carbene effect [65] and the cation effect [66]. The first mainly focuses on the imidazole-based carbene, which possesses strong interaction with CO2 molecule thus could reduce the reaction barrier [67]. In this regard, the formation of carbene depends on the deprotonation by a strong base [65], or extra charges from the cathode [67]. For the cation effect, a thin layer of imidazole-based cations is formed near the metal surface causing strong electron polarization which facilitates CO2RR [32,66]. Two kinds of cationic layers, the intermediate (i.e. adsorbed COOH, *COOH)-induced cationic layer [32] and the cathodic-potential-induced cationic layer [66] have been proposed. The intermediate-induced cationic layer leads to the generation of C1 (mainly CO and HCOO–) products, and anions have a negligible effect on CO2RR performance [32]. The cathodic-potential-induced cationic layer needs a high concentration (e. g. 1 mol L− 1) of free cations [66]. In this study, Cu@PIL with halides exhibit strong chemical adsorption of CO2 (Fig. 3d) in the absence of both strong bases and extra charges. Besides, Cu@PIL-F-1.2 and Cu@PIL-Cl-1.2 mainly provide C2+ products at –0.95 V while Cu@PIL-X-1.2 with other anions (X = Br–, I–, BF4–, and PF6–) produce CH4 under the same condition. Moreover, the imidazolium cations are quasi-static since they are highly decorated in the cross-linked skeleton of PIL. These results indicate there are remarkable differences between the present PIL-metal interface and the conventional IL-metal interface,

thereby influencing the CO2RR process. Herein, we supposed the PIL at the Cu@PIL hybrids may have two
major effects on the CO2RR electrolysis, including the enrichment of CO2 and regulating the product selectivity. The former can be attributed to the outer layer of PILs by functioning as a CO2 enrichment channel, while the latter is mainly imposed by the PIL-Cu interface (or inner layer of PIL) since pure PIL possesses very poor CO2RR performance (Fig. S19). By N 1s XPS results (Fig. 2b), the imidazolium cations decorated in PIL were partially retained during the formation of Cu@PIL. To ascertain if they promote the enrichment of CO2, cross theoretical studies were conducted. Firstly, the intrinsic characteristics of anions were investigated. Evidently, the size of anion increases in the sequence of F– < Cl– < Br– < I– < BF4– < PF6– when the total electron density with the same iso-surface value is considered as the criteria (Fig. S25). However, the charge distribution of BF4– and PF6– differs from halides, that is each F atom possesses –0.299 and –0.252 charges in BF4– and PF6–, respectively, indicating distinct cation-anion electrostatic interaction when contact with cation. The energy of the highest occupied molecular orbital (EHOMO) is associated with the ionization potential, which is a strict criterion for evaluating the electron-donating ability [68]. Interestingly, F– has the highest EHOMO of 2.103 eV (Fig. S26 and Table S5) which means high electron-donating ability, although the electronegativity of the F element is high [69]. PF6– has the lowest EHOMO of –5.301 eV, implying quite poor ability to donate electrons, albeit the same formal charge with F– anion. Subsequently, 1,3-dimethyl
imidazolium cations ([DMIm]+) with different anions are used to investigate the cation-anion electrostatic attraction within the layer of PIL because the imidazolium cations are relatively rigid owing to the large steric hindrance of IL monomer and the highly cross-linked structure of PIL. Upon optimization, all anions are located upon the imidazole ring plane and close to the C2-position (Fig. S27). The distance between this C2 atom and anions increased in the order of F– (1.51 Å) < Cl– (2.41 Å) < Br– (2.65 Å) < I– (2.96 Å) < BF4– (3.02 Å) < PF6– (3.48 Å), corresponding to the weaker interaction sequence. Compared to the F–
alone, that near the imidazolium cation only possesses electrons of 0.244, demonstrating the number of electrons transferred (NET) from F– to the cation is 0.756 (Table S6). However, for PF6–, the NET is only 0.248. These results are consistent well with the N 1s XPS spectra, wherein the BEs of N atoms of imidazolium increased in the sequence of F– < Cl– < Br– < I– < BF4– < PF6– (Fig. 2b), signifying the reduction of electron density. Noteworthily, it has been documented that the reaction of CO2 molecule with imidazolium cations bearing extra charges is thermodynamically favorable [67]. Thus, Cu@PIL-F-1.2 has the best CO2 enrichment than the others. Besides this anion effect, the carbene effect for catching CO2 cannot be completely excluded since the electrolysis was conducted in the alkaline electrolyte.
The in-situ Raman test was performed to study the interfacial properties of Cu@PIL with applied cathodic potential and flowing KOH (1 M) electrolyte and CO2 gas. As shown in Fig. 5a, at the open circuit potential (OCP), two broad peaks at ~522 and ~621 cm− 1 attributed to Cu2O can

be observed. These spectral features decayed rapidly once the negative cathodic potentials were applied, and almost all the surface oxide was reduced to Cu(0) at − 0.1 V. At a more negative potential range from − 0.3 to − 0.9 V, the peak at ~531 cm− 1 attributable to the surficial CuOx and Cu(OH)y species arose, agreeing with the recent literature reported by Jiao’s group [70], in which Cu NPs, chemically deposited Cu (Chem-Cu), and oxide-derived Cu (OD-Cu) all have similar features at the negative potential. After the cathodic potential was removed, peaks related Cu2O appeared immediately, suggesting rapid re-oxidization of the Cu surface (Fig. S28), which is consistent with Gao’s document [64]. This also agrees with the recent results reported by Lei et al. that the high C2+ selectivity of Cu-based catalyst are not associated with a specific oxidation state because all the Cu species (oxides and hydroxides) have been reduced to Cu(0) during the CO2RR [71].
It’s worth noting that the peak at 376 to 368 cm− 1 persists in all the conditions whether the cathodic potential was applied or not, suggesting this feature should be originated from the specific interfacial structure (e.g., Cu species coordinated to pyridinic and imidazolium groups). Two peaks at 295~307 and 355 cm− 1 are assigned to the absorbed CO on Cu (Cu− CO) [64,72]. These two peaks only appeared with the applied cathodic potentials (Fig. S28), suggesting only the reduced Cu species in Cu@PIL have the CO2RR catalytic activity. At higher wavenumbers (>1700 cm− 1), a clear Raman peak at ~2090 cm− 1 arose at 0.2 V, which corresponds to stretching vibration mode of *CO at the top configuration [64,71,73]. This peak quickly disappeared at higher current densities (i. e., at cathodic potential more negative than − 0.1 V), suggesting fast reduction kinetics of this key intermediate [64,73]. Spectral features correspond to the PIL, such as the vibration modes of C− C chain and pyridinic and imidazolium rings, are mainly shown in Fig. 5b, and the assignments of Raman peaks are listed in Table S7.
To study the interfacial structure of Cu@PIL and clarify the effect of the inner layer of PIL, an interface model was built, wherein the crosslinking agent (i.e. DVB) and the IL monomers away from the Cu surface were omitted to reduce the computational consumption. Representatively, a pyridinic group and two imidazolium groups are bonded to the Cu surface, as schematic illustration for XPS results in Fig. 2b and 2c. As a result, the pyridinic group and one of the imidazolium rings are
perpendicular to the Cu surface, while the other imidazolium ring is located parallelly for all anions (Fig. 6). A strong interaction occurs at the interface, resulting in a significant accumulation of electron density (the yellow regions) between the IL monomer and Cu atoms. Notably, the polarized electron density around the perpendicular pyridinic and imidazolium groups is mainly gathered at the N–Cu and C–Cu bonds which are imposed by strong coordination, while that around the paralleled imidazole ring is delocalized (Fig. S29 and S30). Anions can alter the electron density of the interface polarized by the paralleled imidazolium since the NET decreased in the order of F– (0.756) > Cl– (0.505) > Br– (0.486) > I– (0.465) > BF4– (0.272) > PF6– (0.248) (Fig. S27 and Table S5). Such varied interfacial electron density influences the electrolysis pathway by stabilizing the highly polarizable intermediates, such as adsorbed CO2 (*CO2) [74], *COOH [32], and *CO, in different degrees.
Collectively, the characteristics of this newly developed Cu@PIL system can be summarized into three aspects (Fig. 7a): i) The mass transfer of CO2 to the catalytic site is improved by the “individual” ionic pairs in which the exposed imidazolium groups for the enrichment and thereafter pre-activation of CO2. ii) The interfacial electric fields adjacent to the Cu surface are composed of imidazolium cations decorated in a rigid PIL skeleton, which could stabilize the polarized intermediates through the field-dipole interaction [32,66,75–77]. iii) The CO2 enrichment and the stabilization of the polarized intermediate by the PIL shell can be readily adjusted through tuning the anion structure, thus regulating the current density and selectivity of CO2RR. Besides, we also supposed the decoration of a tridentate site in the PIL delivers an active organic-inorganic interfacial structure of Cu@PIL, consisting of the chelate Cu-species with tunable redox property. The concentration of chelated Cu-species varies with anions (Fig. 2b), which thus influences the charge distribution of Cu species at the surface during the electrolysis and the selectivity of CO2RR. Further studies to verify this point will be conducted in the future. Meanwhile, the basic pyridinic groups at the outer layer of PIL may also facilitate the enrichment of CO2.
Specifically, the imidazolium cations of Cu@PIL-F-1.2 possess the largest extra charges since the F– counter anion has the highest NET value, which results in the best CO2 enrichment (Fig. 3d and 7b).

Similarly, the imidazolium cations adjacent to the PIL-Cu interface are closer to electrically neutral, corresponding to a low-intensity electric field. As a result, CO is generated once the *CO is formed due to the weak interfacial stabilization. And Cu@PIL-F-1.2 has the highest current density with the major product of CO at –0.55 V. In comparison, the stabilization of *CO is stronger for Cl– anion, which is beneficial to the formation of dimers, thus improving the C2+ selectivity. On the other hand, PF6– anion exhibits the weakest charge donation effect, leading to a poor CO2 supply. It not only decreases the current density but also facilitates the HER process. Besides, the high-intensity interfacial electric field for Cu@PIL-PF6-1.2 inhibits the desorption and migration of *CO.
Thus, the non-polar product CH4 is generated with the addition of the abundant H source.

sections.heading: 3.5. Electrocatalytic performance with different conditions
sections.text:
The catalytic performance of Cu@PIL-F-1.2 with different cathodic potential was examined (Fig. 8a). The FE of CO decreased from ~60 % to ~30 % with shifting the cathodic potential from –0.45 V to –1.25 V. Noteworthily, only traces of HCOO– are generated at the cathodic potential negatively over –0.75 V, accompanied with an increasing FE of C2H4. Specifically, the FE of C2H4 is less than 10 % at –0.45 V, while it

reaches the maximum value of ~25 % at –1.05 V. Overall, the main products at low potential positively over –0.75 V are the C1 species, such as CO and HCOO–. In contrast, the C2+ products, including C2H4, CH3COO–, and CH3CH2OH, are mainly generated at high potential negatively over –0.75 V. This suggests the stabilization of *CO at Cu@PIL-F-1.2 is so weak that plenty of *CO are desorbed rather than coupled even *CO is generated at a high rate, which consistent with the calculation results (Fig. 6). Further, the rapid growth of current density is also achieved. A high current density of ~590 mA cm− 2 with a low FE of H2 (~22 %) was obtained at –1.25 V, implying not only the mass transfer of CO2 but also the selectivity towards CO2RR is improved by this novel organic-inorganic hybrid.
The influence of electrolyte solution was also evaluated (Fig. S31). The CO2RR performances in KCl (2 M) and KHCO3 (1 M) solutions are quite poor compared to that in KOH (1 M) solution. The former two cases provide relatively high selectivity toward HER (FE of H2 > 40 %), demonstrating Cu@PIL-F-1.2 is pH-specific and it is more suitable to be used in a highly basic rather than a neutral solution. This differs from the recent study by Dai’s group, in which Cu-based catalyst exhibited high activity and selectivity in 2 M KCl solution [78]. The CO2RR performance of Cu@PIL-F-1.2 in KOH solution with higher concentrations was studied (Fig. 8b). As expected, an increase in FE of C2H4 is observed with the raise of KOH concentration. A high FE of C2+ products (58 %) is approached in KOH (3 M) with a high C2+ partial current density of 174 mA cm− 2, which is higher than most of the documented values on Cu-based catalyst (Table S9). Compared with other reported polymer-modified catalyst (Table S10), only Cu@PIL and perfluorosulfonic acid (PSFA) resin-modified Cu exhibit industrial current densities with high C2+ selectivity, signifying the superiority of ionic polymers for CO2RR. The FE of C2+ drops in 5 M KOH electrolyte
solution. As shown in Fig. S32, the FE of H2 increases abruptly and the FE of C2H4 decreases continuously in three consecutive repeated trials, implying the decay of Cu@PIL-F-1.2 in this strongly alkaline solution. Long-time stability was next evaluated. During preliminary experiments, serious flooding and carbonate precipitation were observed after continuous electrolysis at 300 mA cm− 2 for 3 h (Fig. S33) and the catalytic performance continuously deteriorated, which is consistent with the previous studies in which similar commercial GEDs were used [79, 80]. To address this issue, the CO2RR experiments with a lower current density (150 mA cm− 2) in KOH (1 M) were repeated with a sufficient wash of the microporous layer of GDE, followed by dryness at intervals of 3 h (Fig. 8c). A weak fluctuation in cathodic potential of around –0.73 to -0.76 V is observed and the product distribution can be repeated after washing, demonstrating the high durability of the catalytic system. Further efforts including those of improving the water-management by PIL structural design and developing specific GDE for CO2RR in KOH solution are required to promote the stability at high current density (> 150 mA cm− 2) since 240 h stability has been recently reported despite its current density is less than 20 mA cm− 2 [81]. The utilization rate of CO2 was finally evaluated. As shown in Fig. S34, the utilization rate of CO2 continues to decline with the increase of CO2 inlet flow rate and remains unchanged for a long time with a specific inlet flow rate. However, the utilization rate of CO2 is less than 10 % at 150 mA cm-2 in KOH (1 M) even with the lowest CO2 inlet flow rate of 13 mL min-1. This value is worse than that (~30 %) in KHCO3 (1 M) [82], implying the overall CO2RR economic efficiency in strong alkaline system should not be the best even though the selectivity towards C2+ products is better.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text:
In summary, a strategy of constructing Cu@PIL hybrids with the core-shell skeleton was proposed to enhance the current density and broaden the product scope for IL-based CO2RR. To this end, a novel IL monomer comprising a tridentate site, consisting of one pyridinic and two imidazolium groups, and two vinyl sites for polymerization was synthesized, which was used to modify the surface of Cu NPs via in-situ radical polymerization. All Cu@PIL hybrids exhibit the capability to reduce CO2 in-depth (> 2e–), but with varied performance depending on the anions. Upon a combination of experimental exploration and theoretical studies, the high current densities are attributed to the CO2 enrichment promoted by the PIL outer layer. Besides, the interfacial electric field was imposed by the adjacent imidazolium cations that stabilize the polarized intermediates during the electrolysis. Most importantly, the anion effect on both the CO2 enrichment and intermediate stabilization is rationally correlated to the different electrondonating numbers from the respective anion to the imidazolium counterpart. The reaction route with *CO as the key intermediate is proposed, which further signifies the anion effects on the product distribution. Based on our studies, two major differences between the present Cu@PIL system and the conventional bulk IL-based system could be summarized. Firstly, both the intermediate-induced and cathodicpotential-induced imidazolium-based cationic layers can attract electrons from inner atoms of the metal surface [32,66]. For Cu@PIL, the interfacial electric field can be set up with no adsorbed intermediate or applied potential because the imidazolium cation is forced to approach the Cu surface by a rigid PIL skeleton. Namely, the interfacial electric field is structurally induced. Secondly, the adsorbed intermediates other than H (which is not polarized [83]) can be stabilized by this structure-induced interfacial electric field, and the stabilization degree can be regulated by the anions. By contrast, the interfacial electric field is intermediate-specific (i.e. *COOH- specific) for the bulk IL-based system [32]. This work not only demonstrates the new strategy to enhance the current density and broaden the product scope for IL-based CO2RR, but also provides an experimental practice in the application of organic-inorganic hybrid in the value-added chemical synthesis.
